Bautzen
BOWT-sen
n. (the Upper Lusatian capital whose cathedral of Saint Peter has been shared by Catholic and Lutheran congregations since 1524, the oldest such arrangement in Germany)
From Upper Sorbian Budyšin, a Slavic settlement name, Germanised as Bautzen.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Bautzen is the capital of Upper Lusatia and the chief town of the Sorbs, the Slavic people of eastern Germany, whose language it still carries on its street signs. The Reformation came to the city in the fifteen-twenties, and in 1524 an arrangement was made for the collegiate church of Saint Peter which has lasted five hundred years: the chapter kept the choir for the Latin mass and the city took the nave for Lutheran preaching, with a barrier between them. It is the oldest simultaneum in Germany and the church is still shared. Bautzen also printed the first books in Upper Sorbian, and the Sorbian New Testament of 1706 by Michal Frencel was made there for a people of perhaps a hundred thousand. The dictionary records Bautzen for both facts and ranks the second higher. A shared building is a workable arrangement between confessions that cannot agree. A New Testament in the language of a small Slavic people is the thing the Reformation was for.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a nave as the body of a church; a choir as the part where the singers are placed; a partition as that which divides; a dialect as the form of a language in a province; and a version as a translation.

expand to see more

NAVE, n. The middle or body of a church, extending from the balluster or railing of the door to the chief choir.

CHOIR, n. A collection of singers; the part of a church appropriated to the singers, separated from the chancel and nave.

PARTITION, n. That which divides or separates; a dividing wall; the act of dividing.

DIALECT, n. The form or idiom of a language peculiar to a province, or to a kingdom or state; the language of a province.

VERSION, n. A translation; the act of translating; the rendering of a work from one language into another.

Key Scripture

Act 2:8 — "And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?"

1Co 14:9 — "So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air."

Rev 7:9 — "After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;"

Eph 2:14 — "For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us;"

Modern Corruption

Upper Lusatian capital whose collegiate church has been shared by Catholic and Lutheran congregations since 1524, and where the Sorbian New Testament was printed in 1706.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the gospel belongs in small languages. The Sorbs numbered a hundred thousand or so and had no state, no court and no prospect; Bautzen printed their New Testament anyway. Pentecost settles the principle in the form of a question from the crowd: “And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?” (Act 2:8), and Paul makes intelligibility the test of any speech in the assembly, since otherwise “ye shall speak into the air” (1Co 14:9).

The second paragraph names the live temptation, which is to count languages worth translating by the size of the market. John's vision of the redeemed is counted the other way, “a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Rev 7:9). As to the barrier in the middle of Saint Peter's, the dictionary allows it as a civil arrangement and will not call it unity, because what Christ is said to have done is the opposite of building one: he “hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us” (Eph 2:14). A shared roof is peaceable. It is not the same thing as one body.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek dialektos (G1258), a language; Greek glossa (G1100), a tongue; Greek mesotoichon (G3320), a middle wall.

expand to see more

Greek dialektos (G1258) — a language, a dialect; “how hear we every man in our own tongue”, Acts 2:8.

Greek eusemos (G2154) — well marked, distinct, intelligible; “ye shall speak into the air”, 1 Corinthians 14:9.

Greek glossa (G1100) — a tongue, a language; “of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues”, Revelation 7:9.

Greek ochlos (G3793) — a crowd, a multitude; “a great multitude, which no man could number”, Revelation 7:9.

Greek mesotoichon (G3320) — a middle wall, a partition; “hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us”, Ephesians 2:14.

Usage

"“how hear we every man in our own tongue” (Act 2:8) — the principle Pentecost settles."

"“a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Rev 7:9) — how languages are counted."

"“hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us” (Eph 2:14) — why a shared roof is not unity."
